newsitem.title: USA: Williams defense rests, US case to jury on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Williams defense rests, US case to jury on Friday.

text.p: Lawyers for lobbyist Jack Williams rested their case without calling any witnesses Thursday to underscore their argument he did not mislead an investigation into former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
Attorney Barry Levine announced, "The defense rests" seconds after lead prosecutor Robert Ray formally ended government presentation of evidence in U.S. district court.
Closing arguments were set for 0930 EST/1330 GMT Friday.
Williams faced two criminal counts of making false statements when asked about an Espy trip and a scholarship to his girlfriend.
"They didn't prove their case," Levine told reporters. "They (investigators) had this plan of what was important to know and failed to ask them. They are blaming their failure on him (Williams)."

Williams was the Washington lobbyist for Tyson Foods when Espy attended a pro football game in Dallas on January 16, 1994, as a Tyson Foods guest and during the time when Espy's girl friend, Patricia Dempsey, was awarded a $1,200 scholarship by the Tyson Foundation.

Investigators for the Agriculture Department and the FBI said Williams told them he knew nothing about the trip other than what he read in the newspapers and did not even know Dempsey's telephone number.
Other witnesses said Williams paid for Dempsey's airplane ticket for the trip and told Tyson headquarters when she would arrive in Dallas. He also relayed a scholarship application to her by fax.
While the jury was out of the courtroom, Levine asked U.S. District Judge James Robertson to acquit Williams. Robertson deferred a ruling on the request.

Levine faulted investigators for not tape-recording their interviews or keeping a verbatim account. Without it, he said, it would be impossible for jurors to know what was asked and if Williams responded accurately.
"They (investigators) have got to probe and in this case they assiduously avoided it," Levine said.
Prosecutor Ray said it was illegal to make false statements whether they were recorded or not.
"He was asked specific questions that required truthful answers," Ray said, but Williams took an "affirmatively deceptive approach."

Legal experts have said the outcome of the Williams trial may be key to the ongoing investigation of Espy by independent counsel Donald Smaltz. So far, the investigation has resulted in more than a dozen indictments against individuals and concerns but it suffered a setback with the dismissal earlier this month of a related case against Espy's brother, Henry.
Henry Espy was accused of conspiring to accept illegal campaign contributions.
